events.title: The death of William Tyndale
events.shortBlurb: Strangled and burned at Vilvoorde for giving England the Scriptures in her own tongue, Tyndale left a translation that underlies the English Bible to this day…
body: Tyndale, a priest formed at Oxford and Cambridge, held that the plowboy should know the Scripture as well as the prelate. Driven abroad, he translated the New Testament from the Greek and began printing it at Cologne in 1525; stopped there, he finished the work at Worms, and in the summer of 1526 three thousand copies were smuggled into England.

For a decade he lived in hiding on the Continent, adding the Pentateuch and Jonah to his work, while the bishops burned his books and the king's agents hunted him. Betrayed at Antwerp by a false friend, he was held in the castle of Vilvoorde near Brussels and condemned for heresy.

On 6 October 1536, by the reckoning of his earliest biographers, he was strangled at the stake and his body burned, crying — so the martyrologist Foxe records — "Lord, open the King of England's eyes." Within three years an English Bible stood in every parish church; and his renderings, revised but never replaced, still form the bone and sinew of the English versions.
